extracted.intended_audience: readers of The Spectator; teachers, theatre-goers, playwrights, and general readers interested in education and literary taste
extracted.subtask_description: Essays offering prescriptive guidance on theatrical taste, musical appropriateness, methods of educating youth in virtue, and principles of sublime poetic style (drawing on Longinus, Milton, Horace, Xenophon, Apuleius).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix comic epilogues with tragic plays
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid the 'most unnatural Tack of the Comick Tail to the Tragick Head' — attaching a ludicrous epilogue to a serious tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing a merry epilogue onto a tragic performance disrupts the audience's sustained emotion, leaving minds 'jumbled together, and divided between Jest and Earnest.' It undercuts the tragic impact and makes noble sentiments appear 'silly and romantick.' The writer should preserve emotional unity and not trivialize tragic effects with comedic after-pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep musical and performative tone appropriate to the place and business
rubrics_metrics.description: Musicians (and performers) must 'suit their Airs to the Place and Business' and keep to the text like the preacher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epilogues that encourage light, unrelated music can lead to inappropriate practices (e.g., organists ending a sermon with a merry jig), dissipating the congregation's disposition. Performers and musicians should match tone and content to context (church services, tragedies, etc.) to avoid undermining the intended moral or emotional effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach pupils to form right judgment by requiring opinions and reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: When boys read the lives and actions of great men, they should be asked their opinion of an action or saying and obliged to give reasons why they deem it good or bad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This exercise strengthens judgment in virtues such as courage, temperance, honour, and justice — moving beyond mere language comprehension to moral reasoning. Regularly demanding reasons trains boys to discern moral quality rather than parrot textual meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not recommend an exemplar in gross; teach both virtues and faults of models
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid recommending any particular person 'in gross'; instead teach wherein such a man, though great in some respects, was weak and faulty in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without this caution, pupils may be dazzled by a great character and confound its beauties with blemishes. Teachers should dissect models, noting both merits and defects, to prevent uncritical admiration and imitation of moral failings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use analytic moral-writing exercises instead of rote themes or copying
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace or supplement regular themes or copies of verses with tasks that require a boy to write his opinion on persons and actions encountered in reading, to censure or approve specific actions, and to explain improvements or comparisons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign such essays once or twice weekly: have pupils mark moral elements in speeches, assess characters, and argue judgments. This builds moral discernment and strengthens judgment more effectively than mechanical composition exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporary examples of vice's misfortune to deter youth (Horace's method)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set before youth the infamous or honourable characters of contemporaries; let the misfortunes of vice teach avoidance of luxury and extravagance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Horace's reported parental method — illustrating vice by the miserable condition of real people — frightens youth from vice by showing its tangible consequences. Teaching via contemporary, concrete examples promotes prudence and moral caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employ peer-judgment and mutual accusation as moral training (Xenophon)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow Xenophon's model where children spent time hearing mutual accusations and learned to give judgment for offences such as violence, cheating, slander, or ingratitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regularly practicing mutual accusation and adjudication trains children in principles of justice and the exercise of judgment. Making students judge peers' conduct develops civic and moral understanding alongside academic learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use daily accountability and exclusion for idleness (Apuleius / Gymnosophists)
rubrics_metrics.description: Masters inquire of each scholar how he spent the morning; those who cannot account for useful employment are excluded from company and put to work while others dine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This enforces daily responsibility and rewards industry. Institutionalizing public account-giving creates incentives for productive behaviour and immediate consequences for idleness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entrust pupils with secrets to cultivate fidelity and trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Form youth by giving them confidence and responsibilities (as Telemachus was entrusted with secrets), thereby inspiring them not to betray what is committed under the seal of secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treating a pupil like an adult by confiding in him strengthens his sense of honour and fidelity. Practically, involve learners in confidential tasks to train discretion and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give small monetary tasks with reporting and a charity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Occasionally give pupils sixpence apiece and require next-day accounts of its use, with a stipulated fraction (e.g., one-third) reserved for charity and judgment on their choice of object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This concrete exercise promotes prudence, charity, and accountability; rewarding or blaming pupils based on their explanation reinforces moral choices and stewardship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Masters should fashion manners as diligently as they form tongues
rubrics_metrics.description: Schoolmasters ought to take as much care in forming the manners of scholars as in forming their tongues to learned languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neglecting moral formation in favour of mere linguistic instruction risks producing learned men without virtue. The priority of virtue over classical languages (Locke's point) is emphasized: educators should balance intellectual and moral education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve emotional unity in theatrical experience (audience management)
rubrics_metrics.description: An audience's sustained feeling during a dramatic performance should not be dissipated by unrelated levity or incongruous afterpieces; spectators may wish to 'carry some of' the play's melancholy home with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Playwrights and theatre managers should respect the emotional arc they create—avoid contrivances that immediately negate or trivialize the play's intended passions at the close (e.g., jolly epilogues after serious tragedy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sublimity of sentiment does not require passion (Longinus' observation)
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be loftiness in sentiments where there is no passion; the Pathetick may animate the Sublime but is not essential to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers aiming for the sublime can achieve majesty through composed, dignified expression rather than merely inflamed passion. Miltons' Seventh Book exemplifies a 'sedate Majesty' that fills the mind without tumult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitate celebrated authors appropriate to the subject (without servile copying)
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed in the sublime manner, one should 'imitate the most celebrated Authors who have gone before him' and consider how a predecessor (e.g., Homer) would have handled the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitation sparks stylistic elevation when done by catching the spirit of great models rather than slavishly copying. Use selected examples from masters to inform diction, grand ideas, and compositional strategies suited to the work's nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fit allusions and sources for weighty subjects (scriptural/model selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: For high subjects (like creation), use sublime material properly suited (e.g., Milton's allusions to Scripture and the prophets to raise majestic conceptions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate selection of high-register sources (biblical passages, revered authorities) supplies images and ideas that naturally elevate a work; misuse or mismatch of such allusions would weaken solemnity and appropriateness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose tone to match the kind of sublimity required (calm majesty vs. tumult)
rubrics_metrics.description: Different sublime effects call for different styles: composed sedate majesty (Milton's seventh book) versus turbulent, passion-filled grandeur (the sixth book's 'troubled Ocean').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the subject requires tranquil, expansive sublimity or agitated, passionate sublimity and craft diction, rhythm, and imagery accordingly to produce the intended imaginative effect.
